10:00:00:02 - 10:00:25:19 Daniel Winter German carmakers built their success in Europe and found a growth engine in China. But that model is breaking apart in Europe. Weak demand and high costs are piling on the pressure. Volkswagen alone is cutting 100,000 jobs globally and closing factories in Germany. Meanwhile, Germany's carmakers have seen a collapse in market share in China, once a cornerstone of their growth plans.
10:00:25:21 - 10:00:58:01 Daniel Winter They could go to the US. Mercedes and BMW are investing billions into ramping up their presence there. Is it time for German car companies to abandon China, even turn their focus away from Europe? Is it time for Germany to accept the industry's managed decline? Welcome to the Dip, your podcast for money, power and consequences. I'm Daniel, and I'm happy to be joined now by Anna-Marie Baisden who has led coverage of the automotive industry at research firm BMI since 2005.
10:00:58:07 - 10:01:19:01 Daniel Winter Tracking where global carmakers sell, build and invest. Anna-Marie, thank you very much for taking the time for us today. I want to ask you a kind of personal question first. So if you were to go out today and buy a brand new car, are you just automatically going to buy European or are you now starting to look at China and Chinese vehicles?
10:01:19:03 - 10:01:38:21 Anna-Marie Baisden It's a good question. We were actually recently considering a new car, and honestly, I don't think we would rule out, Chinese brands. You know, we were we were recently at Goodwood Festival of Speed, a lot of Chinese presence there. They were unveiling some of their new models. And it's clear that that bring in a lot of value for money.
10:01:38:21 - 10:01:42:07 Anna-Marie Baisden And so, yeah, I certainly wouldn't rule it out.
10:01:42:09 - 10:02:02:12 Daniel Winter So let's get in kind of the ground floor here and talk about the German car industry first and the difficulties that it's had. So can you like kind of lay out in simple terms, what is the state of the German car industry at the moment? That is German brands as they operate globally?
10:02:02:14 - 10:02:37:08 Anna-Marie Baisden Yeah, of course they're facing so many different challenges really. Here in Europe, you know, sales still haven't got back to pre-pandemic levels. And that means that apart from the the financial impact of that, there are a lot of them are also facing overcapacity issues. We've seen Volkswagen talking about, large numbers of, redundancies and, early retirements as much as possible to, to cut down the numbers, floated the idea of closures, although there was some pushback on that.
10:02:37:08 - 10:02:57:07 Anna-Marie Baisden So they're dealing with this overcapacity issue. And then you've got China, which is the biggest standalone market for a lot of these brands where, things have completely flipped for them. In the last ten years or so, where, you know, you would have a brand like Volkswagen that, led the market with one of its local partners.
10:02:57:09 - 10:03:21:14 Anna-Marie Baisden And, now it's sales of, pretty much halved since 2019. And now the the Chinese brands are just dominating that market. And it's very difficult for any, foreign brands, let alone German ones. So they're facing all of these issues there also, you know, the whole electrification push, a lot of them put billions of euros into this.
10:03:21:14 - 10:03:32:11 Anna-Marie Baisden And now it's not playing out as intended. So a lot of companies are revisiting those plans. So you know, they're just dealing with so many things all at once.
10:03:32:13 - 10:03:47:24 Daniel Winter And is there any sort of, any light there, any positive, any upside? For folks from BMW, Mercedes, all of these, car companies at the moment, do you see any way where they can cling onto some hope?
10:03:48:01 - 10:04:09:07 Anna-Marie Baisden Well, certainly we saw in, the earnings results that came out recently, for the first half of the year, in the second quarter, Europe actually proved to be a bright spot for them. And a lot of that, having just talked about electrification not playing out as expected, a lot of that did actually come from the, electrify electrified market.
10:04:09:07 - 10:04:30:00 Anna-Marie Baisden So you had pure battery electric vehicle sales were up by about 40% in Europe. Plug in hybrids up by around 22%. And they were really able to to capitalize on that. So that was actually one of the bright spots. Whereas before, you know, China had been one of the big growth engines. So that proved to be positive.
10:04:30:00 - 10:04:55:00 Anna-Marie Baisden And you know what we're talking about, electrification, even a market like the US, where federal tax breaks were withdrawn in September last year, hybrid demand has really been growing. And so for those carmakers and a lot of them all European, that already have hybrids in the portfolio, or they've changed their strategy to add more hybrids, they're in a really good position to take advantage of that.
10:04:55:02 - 10:05:07:22 Anna-Marie Baisden And again, in recent results, BMW saw its, plug in hybrid sales in the US rose by about 30% last year. So that's a real area of opportunity for them as well.
10:05:07:24 - 10:05:27:19 Daniel Winter Yeah. And we'll dig into that a bit further as we go. Let's start with China then. What has been the big issue that, German carmakers have faced in China? Because for a while it was a cornerstone of their growth, and they seem to be doing fantastically well. And then something flipped, whether it was slowly or all of a sudden, it feels quite sudden.
10:05:28:00 - 10:05:32:03 Daniel Winter What went wrong for them in China?
10:05:32:05 - 10:05:53:04 Anna-Marie Baisden I don't know if it's a case of what went wrong for them or what went right for the Chinese brands in terms of they got a lot of support from the government. We, we hear this talked about a lot in Europe because now these Chinese brands are coming and taking a real foothold in Europe as well. But they had a lot of this government support, across the whole supply chain.
10:05:53:04 - 10:06:36:05 Anna-Marie Baisden You know, if you look at EVs, for example, it's not just producing the cars. They also dominate a lot of the supply chain, right from the minerals and metals processing for the batteries. And so that as well, the fact that China has moved so quickly towards electric vehicles, that was a real push for them. And now, you know, understandably, with a lot of, brand loyalty from the Chinese consumers as well, and the incentives for buying Chinese brands, we've just seen these Chinese brands dominate, and now they're you would have to say they're further advanced in terms of things like, battery electric vehicles, software defined vehicles.
10:06:36:07 - 10:07:00:22 Anna-Marie Baisden And now it almost feels like that relationships flipped. Whereas, you know, when VW came in and was partnered with a local partner for knowledge sharing, it's almost going the other way. Now we see European brands trying to learn from what those Chinese brands are doing. BMW has partnered with the likes of Huawei and to, to get more into the tech side and to develop that side.
10:07:00:24 - 10:07:05:10 Anna-Marie Baisden So that there's really been a flip of who's learning about the market.
10:07:05:12 - 10:07:24:21 Daniel Winter Yeah, it's a fascinating change. And I think we can think about China in two kinds of ways for these German companies. One is building in China for China, and the other is building in China for export to to third markets. So if we just focus on the in China for China aspect of that, should they just essentially give up on that.
10:07:24:21 - 10:07:34:15 Daniel Winter Now is the race won and the Chinese firms have simply pulled ahead. Should they consider pulling out of the Chinese market altogether? These German companies.
10:07:34:17 - 10:07:56:09 Anna-Marie Baisden I think that would be a real last resort for them, because even though, you know, I talked to my father, sales have fallen. It's still their largest standalone market. It's still, one of their big profit drivers. And I think because they've been there for so long and they've seen what the potential can be if they get it right, they don't necessarily want to lose that.
10:07:56:15 - 10:08:25:24 Anna-Marie Baisden And if anything, we're seeing them doubling down. So you talked about Made in China for China. This is becoming a real strategy focusing on localization. And not just, you know, we're going to use more local supply chain and that kind of thing. But also we're making these models for the Chinese market, for the Chinese consumer. And really trying to implement what they've learned from seeing more of these local models.
10:08:26:01 - 10:08:43:16 Anna-Marie Baisden And so that really seems to underline the fact that they want to be there because it helps them learn more about the market and to try and see what can help them be more competitive. So I think it would be unlikely that we would see them just pull out altogether.
10:08:43:20 - 10:09:07:09 Daniel Winter But a cynic would say, that the market there is kind of stacked against them and that we've seen the direction that it's going in now and that, China is helping its homegrown companies to, to do well. And they are doing well. It's not, simply fakery. They are actually developing products which people want to buy at a high quality level.
10:09:07:11 - 10:09:26:01 Daniel Winter And that's the most important thing. That's why you said, the German companies are now learning from the Chinese companies. But what do you think that their future prospects are in China? If we look at the state of play, and also just how involved the Chinese government is there at helping that homegrown talent?
10:09:26:03 - 10:10:00:14 Anna-Marie Baisden It's certainly going to be a struggle. But I you know, I wouldn't say by any means they can't do it. I think, you know, Volkswagen's already seeing relative success with one of its, locally produced models, already seen the same with its new subbrand. You know, it released a whole new brand specifically for China. So I think they are starting to make headway, whether they can see the same kind of success as the Chinese brands and, the same kind of success they saw before.
10:10:00:16 - 10:10:25:13 Anna-Marie Baisden That's maybe a different matter, because also you have to look at what you know, what's going on in the market as a whole, which is sales are slowing down from, the, the pace of growth we've seen previously in China. So that's something that's going to impact everyone. But there are signs that if they can, you know, really tap into what is successful for the local brands, then there's certainly opportunities.
10:10:25:15 - 10:10:59:23 Daniel Winter Okay. So perhaps some potential still to come in China for the German companies, or at least that if they've still got hope in it. But turning our attention to the US now, BMW has put $1.7 billion into a South Carolina expansion. Mercedes has announced $7 billion, in the US that they're going to invest there by 2030. What does this tell you about the forces that, putting pressure on German car makers in terms of where they decide that they want to expand and build?
10:11:00:00 - 10:11:16:20 Anna-Marie Baisden Yeah, there's certainly a big policy aspect to this. You know, the the US tariffs on imported vehicles have certainly made carmakers have to stop and think about how they will continue doing business, with the US. And so just jumping on that.
10:11:16:20 - 10:11:35:09 Daniel Winter First, so are we saying that a big part of the US sales could be made up by sending cars from the EU that they made in the EU, to the US, and now they're going to, to cut that or cut it more in favor of building in the US. Is that how that shakes out?
10:11:35:11 - 10:12:03:12 Anna-Marie Baisden Well, we started looking at this when the tariffs were implemented. If you look at Porsche, it has smaller volumes than the others. So it may not necessarily be in their interest to start producing, in the US, but certainly those brands that already do produce in the US, they're expanding those facilities or adding to them. And really, it's because the those facilities in the US are not just for the US.
10:12:03:12 - 10:12:26:02 Anna-Marie Baisden Some of them are actually global export bases for certain models, particularly the big, premium SUVs, which sell well in the US. But they also export them. So there is a business case there for investing in the US. But we would say maybe it's they've been nudged a little by the policy that's been put in place.
10:12:26:04 - 10:12:38:24 Daniel Winter Okay. And is there something about the conditions in the US market itself which makes it more attractive or certainly more attractive at the moment than the difficulties that they're having in the Chinese market?
10:12:39:01 - 10:13:05:08 Anna-Marie Baisden Yes. And I think, you know, talking about the fact that they're building, premium SUVs, there are always very different kinds of passenger markets, whereas you had well, particularly for the mass market manufacturers, you know, the North America is very much, light trucks and big SUV's. Whereas if you go ten years ago back to in Europe, it's more hatchbacks, little city cars.
10:13:05:10 - 10:13:28:15 Anna-Marie Baisden If you were a European mass market brand producing those kinds of cars, they didn't sell as well in the US. But now we've seen this almost global consumer shift towards SUVs, and that has really helped. Because it means as well as the premium cars that were already selling well for the likes of, BMW and Mercedes, you know, they've always been, status symbols in the US.
10:13:28:17 - 10:13:38:16 Anna-Marie Baisden Now they can add these kind of bigger volume models as well, like the SUV. So the product mix is a lot more favorable for them to be in the US as well. At the moment.
10:13:38:18 - 10:13:53:04 Daniel Winter Yeah. That's interesting. And you and your team BMI have done a lot of work looking into regionalization in carmakers. And can you explain what it means when we just talk about regionalization and how it is shaping the future of the car industry?
10:13:53:06 - 10:14:19:23 Anna-Marie Baisden Yeah. So this is when we talk about localization of the supply chain. Is that what you referring to? Yes. Yeah. Yeah. So what we've seen and to be honest this is not just around tariffs. There have been so many things over the last few years that have really sparked this. And I think if we go back to Covid as well, it became clear just how reliant a lot of carmakers are on Asia and particularly on China.
10:14:20:00 - 10:14:44:07 Anna-Marie Baisden And because it was difficult, you know, supply chains were really disrupted even when things started opening up again. And so it became clear that, maybe the other big automotive markets such as Europe, such as North America, needed more local supply chains. And so what we've seen, because as you said, we track investment into the manufacturing side of the industry, region by region.
10:14:44:09 - 10:15:12:24 Anna-Marie Baisden And what we've seen is a lot more investment into the supply chain, into EV batteries in some cases. You know, that's now being scaled back in North America, particularly where EV demand isn't what it was expected to be. But certainly we're seeing a lot more investment into localizing those supply chains so that European brands, American brands, they don't have to be as reliant on, one particular region or one particular country.
10:15:13:05 - 10:15:19:22 Anna-Marie Baisden And so if there are disruptions, again, you know, at least their suppliers are closer to them.
10:15:19:24 - 10:15:40:07 Daniel Winter So if, let's say factories in in Germany start closing. Obviously that has a massive effect on the suppliers as well. Is there any sense that some of this business can be picked up elsewhere so that they can move some of these trusted suppliers, that the trusted suppliers are happy to go? With Volkswagen, for example.
10:15:40:09 - 10:15:50:07 Daniel Winter To the US, or is it building entirely a brand new set of, supply chains and partnerships inside that new location?
10:15:50:09 - 10:16:12:09 Anna-Marie Baisden It's certainly possible because we see this a lot, actually, with South Korean brands. They've set up mostly in southern states in the US. And what we've seen is, you know, a little cluster of suppliers, again, the South Korean suppliers that they usually work with setting up their with them. So it wouldn't be unheard of for that to happen.
10:16:12:09 - 10:16:14:03 Anna-Marie Baisden Certainly.
10:16:14:05 - 10:16:35:22 Daniel Winter And now just to kind of focusing in on Germany itself again, I mean, Germany produced, a record 1.67 million electric cars last year, which is second only to China. So is the crisis at the moment being overstated? Would you say?
10:16:35:24 - 10:17:10:07 Anna-Marie Baisden I would say not necessarily, because, yes, that is impressive. It's a record number of electric vehicles, but we're also at a point at the moment where demand can still absorb that kind of production. I think this is one of the concerns is that will it start fading? I mean, I think we already saw EV sales starting to, slow down a little in Europe before we had the Us-Iran conflict, where, fuel prices rose, we saw a lot more interest in electric vehicles.
10:17:10:09 - 10:17:37:22 Anna-Marie Baisden So there is that concern as to whether that's sustainable. And then there's also as, you know, alluded to at the beginning, quite a bit of overcapacity, in terms of, you know, will more about the vehicles that they're not producing anymore. There's still the capacity for those. So I when, you know, you look at the size of the, job cuts that VW is talking about making could be up to 100,000.
10:17:38:02 - 10:17:59:22 Anna-Marie Baisden So I think the concern is definitely real. But, you know, as we were saying, there are certainly some bright spots. It just depends on I think we're kind of at a crossroads as to how this electrification journey is going to play out and whether we can keep this going now or whether it is going to be very cyclical, depending on things like geopolitical events.
10:17:59:24 - 10:18:36:21 Daniel Winter So an uncertain trajectory. But when it comes to the difficulties that, these carmakers are facing in Germany, is it simply down to circumstances? We've seen, for example, high electricity prices, meaning that the cost of production is high in Germany, tough labor laws, all kinds of other things that the companies themselves have mentioned. Is it those circumstances or is it more failure to plan, failure to take risks at the top levels, the executive, levels of these companies and therefore failing to get ahead of the competition?
10:18:36:23 - 10:19:06:11 Anna-Marie Baisden I'd say a little bit of everything in that case, you know, certainly, I think we saw this with, Russia, Ukraine as well, when energy prices rose, and competitiveness really started to take a hit. We started to see how this was going to play out. I don't know if the decision making necessarily, has been too cautious because, as I said, we saw companies put in billions of euros into developing EVs.
10:19:06:13 - 10:19:38:10 Anna-Marie Baisden Maybe it was a little behind the curve, though. When you look at the Chinese industry, and it's also I mean, you know, we hear so much about, Chinese brands coming to Europe and the damage that's doing. But I think the reality is it's so difficult in terms of policy to compete with what the Chinese government's done because, you can have much more centralized, agile decision making in China because it is so centralized government.
10:19:38:10 - 10:19:56:01 Anna-Marie Baisden Whereas Germany, being part of the EU, it takes a lot longer for policy to come through. You have to have all of the the member states in agreement. So there's also an element of that. The policy that's supportive of these big decision, investment decisions hasn't always been there for them.
10:19:56:03 - 10:20:07:07 Daniel Winter And so what are the chances of a of a turnaround. Do you see that there are levers that the government can pull that will genuinely help the German carmakers?
10:20:07:09 - 10:20:27:13 Anna-Marie Baisden I would say there are limits to what the German government itself can do because of being an EU member state. And so a lot of the policy, you know, the the much bigger, policy that will help, such as we saw after Covid. You know, that's a good example of a lot of the supportive policy came at the EU level.
10:20:27:15 - 10:21:03:23 Anna-Marie Baisden Because you can't subsidize national sectors as a member state. So we've seen things certainly from the national level, such as the new, EV incentives that came in at the start of this year. They can do that to support, the EV sales. And actually from the EU level, we're starting to see some of these supportive measures come through, like the Industrial Accelerator Act, which is meant to really focus on localization, as we were talking about earlier, and the sort of made in Europe, support for using more local supply chains.
10:21:04:00 - 10:21:10:24 Anna-Marie Baisden Okay. I would say again, that's very supportive for clean technologies. It doesn't necessarily cover the whole industry.
10:21:11:01 - 10:21:40:15 Daniel Winter Yeah. And so is there some sort of intervention that seems possible? I mean, like on a practical level, not just a theoretical level. From Brussels, in order to, for example, put up tariffs to make it more difficult for China to bring models into the EU. I know, though, they're also setting up factories to actually make, some of these, Chinese models, in the EU, in Hungary, for example, there's a lot of investment being put in there.
10:21:40:17 - 10:21:59:19 Daniel Winter So, so the the difficulty, though, seems to be to get the member states of the EU to actually agree on a common position. So do you even see foresee any sort of pushback coming from the EU in terms of putting up tariffs, for example?
10:21:59:21 - 10:22:28:22 Anna-Marie Baisden Well, VW actually alluded to this in their recent earnings call. And it does seem like an easy win. In terms of adding additional support. The the fact that the tariffs at the moment are on battery electric vehicles on Chinese imported battery electric vehicles, those tariffs don't cover, plug in hybrids. And so as a result, you've now got Chinese brands accounting for around 30% of the plug in hybrid market.
10:22:28:24 - 10:22:53:20 Anna-Marie Baisden Again, a segment which is doing very well in Europe at the moment because they're a little bit cheaper, not as much range anxiety. So, you know, that's been great for the Chinese brand. So if you were to consider that, you know, expanding the tariffs to other segments of the electric vehicle market, that could be that, you know, low hanging fruit in terms of something to do to support the local industry.
10:22:53:22 - 10:23:13:21 Daniel Winter Yeah. You just have to get all of these member states to agree. That seems to be the the big, problem, the big issue there. But if they can, then that could be a massive, lever that they can pull. So kind of bringing this into land a little bit now, do you. Okay. Just just a spicy take.
10:23:13:21 - 10:23:34:21 Daniel Winter You can agree or disagree with it. Do German car companies need to be less German in order to survive? And that could mean do they need to be more Chinese? Do they need to be more American even in order to, move up the next rung of the ladder and, be where they need to be in
